title: A player presses the feedback button, and an AI agent starts preparing the pull request. My workflow as a solo dev.
author: CrossroadsLegends
selftext:
Two years ago I tested how much of an app Cursor could write without me writing a single line of code. The answer back then: not much that stayed working. After I finished the third tab, the first one was already broken again. Missing context, no real verification loops, working features breaking again and again.

This year I started a game, Crossroads Legends, a location-based RPG with d20 combat, now in closed beta. I want to share how differently it works now, because this sub is about exactly that.

Start. January, Opus 4.5 and ChatGPT, me describing, reviewing and pasting code by hand. In March I ran a 14-day alpha with about 30 players, and after that progress got slow. The tools were still not good enough for a project this size. Only in the last weeks did the workflow quality get to where going all in was worth it.

Feedback to pull request. The feedback button in the game sends to an n8n workflow. n8n creates a GitHub issue, and that starts a headless Opus session that looks at the issue and the code and prepares a PR on its own. I review and merge. Sometimes the PR is ready before I've read the feedback. For me that's the most interesting part: how much software development can change if you let it.

Coding. A handful of agents in parallel (Claude Code, Codex and Jarvis, an agent I built myself). For bigger features I split the work by layer: database and types, server, admin panel, client UI. Shared TypeScript interfaces first, then each agent gets its own git worktree. One feature for the roguelike dungeons shipped as 4 PRs from 4 agents on the same day.

QA. A test agent plays the game for 24 hours: screenshot, Claude Haiku decides what it sees and what to do next, no hardcoded selectors. It files issues to GitHub and writes hourly reports.

What went wrong. In July an audit found 70 issues, some of them critical exploits, all with the same root cause: I trusted client input. Fixed in one week (server tests 171 → 928, client 58 → 304). The lesson for me: the answer to agent-made bugs was not fewer agents, but a second pass that checks the first one before you trust either.

Of course, not everything works on the first try, and faster development doesn't automatically mean a better game. That's why I need players. The current playtest has about 14 testers and the feedback is promising, but I want people who don't know me and will be honest. If you want to try it, or pick apart the workflow: [crossroadslegends.com](http://crossroadslegends.com)

Is anyone else connecting player feedback directly to agents? Where did it break for you?

comments.author: randommmoso
comments.body: Your website bored me to death. Nobodys reading all this shit. Dont you know you need to convince people to click play? Why are you even calling it closed beta? Just get some people playing it. Why isn't gameplay immediately presented when I first click? Why do I need to read all this?

comments.author: randommmoso
comments.body: After reading all of this i think you are not really interested in building a game. Why dont you automate players and basically have your own little fake kingdom? If you dont want to read the feedback I give you why would I want to waste my time? Does that make sense? Or will claude reply for you?

replies.author: CrossroadsLegends
replies.body: thanks for the honest feedback. working on the website content now
